youtube.aciklama:
How is an auditory-verbal therapy session planned and run? In this lesson we cover writing goals in five areas, the steps of parent coaching, acoustic highlighting, the listening first principle, learning to listen sounds and how progress is monitored.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Estabrooks, MacIver-Lux and Rhoades, Auditory-Verbal Therapy: Science, Research, and Practice; AG Bell Academy for Listening and Spoken Language, Principles of LSLS Auditory-Verbal Therapy; Erber, Auditory Training; Tye-Murray, Foundations of Aural Rehabilitation: Children, Adults, and Their Family Members.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Goals, parent coaching, acoustic highlighting, monitoring
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how an auditory-verbal therapy session is planned and how it is run step by step.
We will cover parent coaching, acoustic highlighting, the listening first principle and how progress is monitored.
In most programs, auditory-verbal sessions are weekly, last about an hour, and the parent is always in the session.
Before the session, the therapist plans the goals and the play activities that will target them.
The session starts with a short listening check showing the device or implant works; we will see the Ling sounds in the next lesson.
Then games that interest the child are played in turn, each working on several goals together.
In most activities the parent also plays with the child; the therapist watches, guides and gives feedback.
The session ends by discussing with the parent what worked and setting home goals for the week.
So the main work happens not in the session, but at home during the rest of the week, within daily life.
In auditory-verbal therapy, goals are usually written in five developmental areas; the first is listening.
The second area is speech; the aim is for the child to produce vowels, consonants and sound patterns.
The third area is language: vocabulary and grammar at the levels of understanding and use.
The fourth area is cognition; thinking, concept development, symbolic play and auditory memory belong here.
The fifth area is communication: turn taking, eye contact, asking questions and keeping a conversation going.
A single game can target several areas together; for example, a farm animal game combines listening, words and turn taking.

maddeler.metin: Can be used at home too

cumleler: Goals are based on the child's latest assessment and the parent's observations at home.
Goals follow the natural order of listening, speech and language development in hearing children.
Each goal is short term and measurable; it states under what condition and with what success it will be done.
A sample goal: the child identifies animal sounds in a closed set of three toys, through listening alone, in four of five trials.
This goal matches the identification step we saw in the auditory skills hierarchy lesson.
A good goal can be used at home; the parent can set up the same game again in the bath or at the table.
In parent coaching, the therapist passes skills on to the parent, making the parent the child's main teacher.
The therapist first briefly explains the goal of the activity and why it matters.
Then the therapist demonstrates the strategy with the child; the parent watches.
Next the parent tries the same activity with the child; the therapist steps back and observes.
Feedback starts with what the parent did well, then focuses on a single small suggestion.
Finally, they agree together on which daily routine at home the strategy will be used in.
Coaching is collaboration, not a lecture; the parent's observations about the child are among the most valuable information.
Instead of judgmental language, the therapist starts from the parent's strengths, which builds the parent's confidence.
The family is asked about its own goals; for example, the child turning around on hearing their name in the park.
Activities are adapted to the family's culture, the features of its language and its daily schedule.
When appropriate, people who spend a lot of time with the child, such as grandparents and siblings, also join the session.
The parent's fatigue and worry are noticed too; if needed, they are referred for psychological support and parent groups.
Acoustic highlighting means making the target word or sound easier for the child to hear.
The target word is said with a little more stress, a little longer and with more melody, after a short pause.
Placing the target word at the end of the sentence also adds emphasis, because the last word is the easiest to remember.
The bars in the graph are an example of word durations when the same sentence is said in an everyday and a highlighted way.
Some therapists also use whispering to bring out voiceless consonants such as s and sh.
As the child progresses, highlighting is reduced; the aim is for the child to understand everyday speech at a natural pace.

maddeler.metin: If missed, visual, then sound again
Pointing out sound: did you hear?
Close to the ear, quiet room

cumleler: Under the listening first principle, a new word or instruction is first presented through hearing alone.
If the child does not understand, visual support such as a picture or object is added, then the words are given again through hearing alone.
We saw in the auditory skills hierarchy lesson that this sequence is called the auditory sandwich.
The therapist and parent often sit beside the child, close to the device microphone, so the child takes in speech through the ear.
When a sound is heard, pointing to the ear and saying did you hear that turns the child's attention to the sound.
The session room is quiet and the speaker stays close to the child's device; distance and noise weaken the sound.

ogeler.metin: Talk about what the child sees

cumleler: Wait time is an important strategy: after a question, the adult waits a few seconds for the child to respond.
When the child says ball, the parent expands it by saying red ball, modeling the next language step.
Offering a choice, such as do you want an apple or a banana, makes it easier for the child to hear and use the word.
The adult talks about the object the child is interested in, because the child's attention is already there.
The same target word is heard many times, in different games and in the voices of different people.
These strategies are not only for the session; the aim is for the parent to use them naturally all day.
With young children, sounds paired with toys are often used; these are called learning to listen sounds.
For example, an airplane is paired with a long aaah, and a cow with a low, melodic moo.
Interrupted sounds such as the train's choo choo teach differences in duration and rhythm.
The snake's sss shows whether the child hears energy in the high frequencies.
The sounds are chosen to differ in features such as low and high, long and short; each language's onomatopoeic words suit this well.
The child uses these sounds as a bridge to first words; over time, the object's name replaces the sound.
The goals worked on in each session and the child's success rate are written in the session note.
A short diary kept by the parent or short videos from home show the child's performance at home.
Listening development is tracked with checklists that order the milestones and with parent questionnaires.
Language and speech are measured with age-appropriate standard tests at set intervals, for example once or twice a year.
Goals are updated based on the results; a child who reaches a goal moves on to the next step.
The general benchmark is at least one year of language growth each year, with the child gradually closing the gap with peers.
If progress is slower than expected, the first question is whether the child really hears speech; the device and fitting are checked.
Data logging shows how many hours a day the device is used; low use directly slows progress.
Recurrent middle ear problems can temporarily reduce the sound heard through the device.
Additional needs such as attention, cognitive development or autism spectrum are assessed; if needed, the child is referred to a specialist.
If progress is still limited despite all this, the communication approach is discussed again with the family.
This is a team decision made together by the audiologist, the therapist and the family.

sahneler.metin: Save the last five minutes of the session for the parent: what worked, in which routine at home, with which single strategy? Write one concrete home goal.
cumleler: A clinical tip: save the last five minutes of the session for the parent alone.
In this time, ask the parent to describe in their own words what worked in the session.
Then decide together which single strategy to use in which routine at home; for example, acoustic highlighting at bath time.
Write the home goal short and concrete, and start the next session by talking about it.

maddeler.metin: Monitoring: at least a year's growth yearly

cumleler: In auditory-verbal therapy, goals are written in measurable form in listening, speech, language, cognition and communication.
In parent coaching, the therapist explains and demonstrates; the parent tries and receives feedback.
Acoustic highlighting and the listening first principle make it easier for the child to take in speech through the ear.
Progress is tracked with session notes, home records and standard tests; if it is slow, audibility is checked first.

sahneler.soru: What does the therapist do in parent coaching?
sahneler.aciklama: The therapist _guides the parent_; the parent is the main teacher.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: what is the therapist's main role during parent coaching in auditory-verbal therapy?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: guiding the parent and giving feedback.
The parent tries the activity with the child, so they can apply what they learn at home all day.
